notes.meaning: Samuel reminds Saul that the Lord sent him to crown him as king over Israel. Because God gave Saul his high position, Saul has a duty to listen to and obey God's commands. This new order gives Saul a fresh opportunity to prove his loyalty as God's ruler.

The Lord remembers how the Amalekite people ambushed Israel when they were coming out of Egypt. They cruelly attacked the weak and tired people who lagged behind. Even though hundreds of years had passed, God never forgot their wicked actions and now brings His judgment.

God commands Saul to attack the Amalekites and destroy everything that belongs to them without showing pity. They are placed under a ban, which means devoting them entirely to God's judgment rather than taking plunder. This war is not meant to make Israel rich, but to carry out God's sentence against a cruel nation.

Saul gathered a huge army of two hundred thousand foot soldiers from Israel and ten thousand men from Judah at Telaim. Gathering so many men showed that he took the task seriously. His fast preparations gave high hopes that he would carry out the mission faithfully.

Saul marched his army to the main city of the Amalekites and set an ambush in the valley. He hid his forces to trap the enemy when the battle began. This was a common battle plan designed to draw the defenders away from their city walls.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note that while early Greek and Latin translations read 'lay in wait,' the traditional Hebrew text says Saul contended or fought in the valley.

notes.meaning: Saul warned the Kenite people to move away from the Amalekites so they would not be caught in the battle. The Kenites were relatives of Moses by marriage and had treated Israel with great kindness in the desert. God remembered their past help and spared them while punishing their wicked neighbors.

Saul struck down the Amalekites across a vast stretch of desert country from Havilah to Shur, near the border of Egypt. His soldiers chased and defeated them across the whole land. Many Amalekites were wiped out, though some fled into neighboring lands.

Saul captured King Agag alive, but he put the rest of the captured Amalekite people to death with the sword. Sparing the enemy king was Saul's first direct violation of God's clear instructions. Saul may have kept Agag as a living trophy to show off his victory.

Saul and his soldiers spared King Agag along with the finest sheep, cattle, and fattened livestock. They were unwilling to give up the best goods, but they willingly destroyed everything that was weak, sickly, or worthless. Saul followed his own greed and judgment instead of obeying God's direct command.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars explain that the Hebrew phrase for fat calves is unusual and likely refers to superior animals born in a second birth.

notes.meaning: The word of the Lord came to the prophet Samuel with a painful revelation. God told His prophet what Saul had done before Samuel ever saw the king. God sees everything people do in secret, and He holds His leaders responsible.

God told Samuel that He regretted making Saul king because Saul had turned away from following His instructions. When God expresses regret, it does not mean He made a mistake, but that Saul's rebellion caused God to change how He dealt with him. Samuel was deeply grieved by this news and spent the whole night crying out to God in prayer.

Samuel got up early in the morning to meet Saul, but he was told that Saul had gone to Carmel to build a stone monument in his own honor. Instead of giving thanks to God, the king was seeking his own fame. After setting up this memorial, Saul marched down to Gilgal in triumph.

When Samuel reached him, Saul welcomed the prophet warmly and boasted that he had carried out all the Lord's instructions. Saul was either fooling himself or trying to hide his guilt before Samuel could challenge him. People who loudly brag about their obedience are often hiding their failures.

Samuel quickly exposed Saul's hollow claim by pointing out the sounds of the captured animals. The bleating of sheep and lowing of cattle were noisy proof that Saul had disobeyed God's command to destroy everything. Saul could not pretend to be faithful when the evidence against him was heard by everyone.

Saul made excuses by blaming the soldiers for sparing the best animals, claiming they did it to sacrifice them to Samuel's God. He tried to hide behind a religious excuse to cover up their selfish greed. Sins cannot be excused by claiming they were done with good intentions.

Samuel told Saul to stop making excuses and listen to what the Lord had revealed to him the night before. The king needed to hear God's true verdict instead of offering more explanations. Even as Samuel prepared to deliver the hard message, Saul told him to speak on.

Samuel reminded Saul of when he was small in his own eyes and had no royal ambition. God was the one who lifted him up and made him king over the tribes of Israel. Because God gave him his throne, Saul owed total obedience to the God who raised him to honor.

The Lord had sent Saul on a clear mission to destroy the sinful Amalekites completely until they were wiped out. God promised victory, making the campaign an assured duty rather than an uncertain war. Saul had no excuse for failing to finish a task where God's instructions were so simple.

Samuel asked Saul why he failed to obey God's voice and instead rushed greedily upon the plunder. Grabbing the spoils for himself was an evil act that showed contempt for God's holy instructions. True evil is choosing our own desires over what God clearly tells us to do.

Saul stubbornly argued that he really had obeyed the Lord by going on the mission and defeating the Amalekites. He even pointed to bringing King Agag back alive as if that proved his faithfulness. In his pride, Saul convinced himself that doing most of what God asked was the same as full obedience.

Saul repeated his excuse that the soldiers took the finest animals only to offer them as sacrifices to the Lord at Gilgal. He claimed that dedicating the plunder to God made their actions acceptable. But God does not accept gifts that are taken by breaking His direct commands.

Samuel told Saul that the Lord delights far more in obedience than in animal sacrifices and burnt offerings. Sacrifices are just religious ceremonies, but listening to God's voice is the true heart of faith. Bringing a gift to an altar is worthless if we refuse to do what God tells us to do.

Samuel warned that rebellion against God is as wicked as witchcraft, and stubbornness is as evil as worshipping false idols. When people insist on their own way against God, they are making an idol out of their own will. Because Saul rejected God's word, God rejected him from remaining king over Israel.

Saul finally admitted that he had sinned, but he quickly blamed his actions on being afraid of the soldiers. He claimed he gave in to their demands instead of standing firm on God's orders. His confession showed that he feared what people thought of him more than he feared God.

Saul pleaded with Samuel to forgive his sin and come back with him so he could worship the Lord. He wanted Samuel to act like a go-between to restore his reputation in public. Saul was far more worried about losing his royal honor than about being truly right with God.

Samuel refused to go back with Saul and repeated God's sentence of rejection. The prophet would not join in an act of worship that made Saul look like a faithful king when he had rebelled. Disobeying God's voice cost Saul his right to rule God's people.

As Samuel turned to leave, Saul grabbed the edge of the prophet's robe in desperation, and the cloth tore. Saul was frantic to keep Samuel by his side so the people would not see their division. The torn robe instantly became an object lesson for what was happening to Saul's reign.

Samuel announced that just as the robe tore, the Lord had torn the kingdom of Israel from Saul that very day. God would give the throne to a neighbor who was better and more faithful than Saul. Although David was not mentioned by name yet, God had already chosen the next king.

Samuel declared that the Glory of Israel does not lie or change His mind like a human being. People change their plans because they are weak or do not know the future, but God has all power and His decrees are sure. God's decision to remove the kingdom from Saul's family was final and would not be undone.

differ.view: God never changes His mind or purposes, so His regret over Saul reflects His holy grief and a change in His actions toward Saul, not an error or surprise.
God genuinely changes His mind and adapts His plans in response to human decisions because He takes real risks with people.

notes.meaning: Saul confessed again that he had sinned, but he begged Samuel to honor him before the elders and the people by returning with him to worship. Saul cared more about saving his public pride than about taking the shame of his sin. Even while admitting his guilt, his focus was on maintaining his political status.

Samuel agreed to go back with Saul, and Saul bowed down to worship the Lord. Samuel returned to prevent panic among the people and to carry out the sentence on King Agag, not to undo Saul's rejection. Saul went through the motions of worship, but his kingdom remained lost.

Samuel commanded that King Agag be brought to him, and Agag approached cheerfully. Agag thought that since the heat of the battle had passed and Saul had spared his life, all danger of death was gone. He falsely believed he was safe, unaware that God's judgment was about to fall.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars translate the verse to mean that Agag came trembling and said death is bitter, realizing that he was about to be executed.

notes.meaning: Samuel told Agag that because his sword had made mothers childless through cruel attacks, his own mother would now be childless. Samuel then executed Agag before the Lord at Gilgal to finish the judgment that Saul had neglected. This act completed God's holy sentence against the wicked Amalekite king.

Samuel went home to Ramah, and Saul returned to his home in Gibeah. The close partnership between the prophet and the king came to an end. Saul went back to his palace, but he no longer had the blessing and guidance of God's prophet.

Samuel never visited Saul again for the rest of his life, though he grieved deeply over Saul's downfall. The Lord regretted making Saul king because Saul had chosen rebellion instead of obedience. God's rejection of Saul was complete, paving the way for a new king to lead Israel.
